turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Number 149! Really, Mr. Worthing, you must endeavour to be more precise. One does not simply state a number without providing context; it suggests a lamentable lack of attention to detail, a quality I find quite… distressing.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Forgive me, Lady Bracknell. I simply assumed... well, it seemed the most straightforward way to convey the information. I assure you, I have the utmost respect for precision, and I deeply regret any distress I may have caused.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Mr. Worthing, your apologies are, of course, accepted, though one hopes such egregious errors will not be repeated. However, let us proceed; we have much ground to cover before I can possibly consider you fit to associate with my daughter. Now, tell me, what is your profession?

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I, uh, I'm a gentleman, Lady Bracknell. I devote my time to… to managing the Cecily Cardew estate in the country, and generally looking after things. It's a rather… absorbing occupation, you see.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: “Managing an estate, you say? A most commendable pursuit, though one is curious as to the precise nature of this ‘management.’ Does it involve, for example, the judicious application of manure, or the overseeing of agricultural labourers? These are matters of vital importance, you understand.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Oh, good heavens, no, Lady Bracknell! My involvement is… rather more supervisory, you see. I mainly ensure that everything runs smoothly, and that the tenants are… comfortable. It’s a delicate balance, really.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: “Comfortable tenants,” Mr. Worthing? A most agreeable sentiment, but scarcely sufficient to demonstrate competence. One does not merely desire comfortable tenants; one requires them to be *productive* tenants, contributing to the overall prosperity of the estate. Pray, enlighten me further on how you achieve this 'comfortable' state, and what precise contribution these tenants make to the Cardew fortune.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Well, Lady Bracknell, I ensure they are comfortable through… through a certain degree of, shall we say, amicable relations? They are, of course, perfectly respectable people, and I believe a happy tenant is a loyal one, which contributes to the estate's stability, wouldn't you agree?

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Amicable relations! Mr. Worthing, you speak as if managing an estate were a mere social tea party, not a serious responsibility! Stability, you say? One achieves stability through sound financial principles, not through cultivating a fondness for one's labourers.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I… I do endeavor to be mindful of financial principles, Lady Bracknell, truly! It’s just that I believe a contented workforce, as it were, is also a productive one, and… and fosters a sense of goodwill, which, I’m sure, ultimately benefits everyone involved.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Goodwill, Mr. Worthing? A sentiment best left to philanthropists and Sunday school teachers! It appears your understanding of estate management is… remarkably unorthodox, and I confess, rather alarming. Pray tell, do you possess any discernible knowledge of the current market value of agricultural produce?

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Agricultural produce, Lady Bracknell? Well, I… I confess, my expertise lies more in the, ah, social sphere, rather than the, the, precise figures involved. I’ve always taken a rather optimistic view of the harvest, hoping for the best, you see!

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Optimism, Mr. Worthing, is a dangerous indulgence, particularly when dealing with turnips! It is scarcely the quality one seeks in a gentleman destined to marry into a respectable family. Let us proceed, then, to a more pertinent line of inquiry.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Indeed, Lady Bracknell. I… I strive to view life with a positive outlook, and I believe it does one good to have hope, even when faced with… turnips. Perhaps I could demonstrate my commitment to sound judgment in another area?

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Hope, Mr. Worthing, is a most unattractive characteristic in a man. It suggests a lack of preparation, a deficiency in foresight, and, frankly, a distressing unwillingness to confront unpleasant realities. Let us, therefore, abandon this frivolous discussion of sentiments and address a matter of considerably more import: your family.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: My family, Lady Bracknell? Yes, of course. It’s… a rather complicated matter, I’m afraid. I’ve always believed in the importance of lineage, though my own circumstances are, admittedly, somewhat… unusual.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Really, Mama, must you interrogate Mr. Worthing so thoroughly? It's dreadfully embarrassing, and quite unnecessary, as I’ve already declared our engagement!

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Unnecessary, my dear Gwendolen? Your declarations are as fleeting as a summer shower and require, I assure you, a degree of rigorous scrutiny. Mr. Worthing, your family is, I trust, not entirely devoid of connection to the landed gentry? One cannot be too particular, you understand.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Goodness, Lady Bracknell, I… I wouldn’t presume to claim any direct connection to the landed gentry, no. My origins are… somewhat obscured, I’m afraid, having been found as a baby in a handbag at Victoria Station. A most unfortunate circumstance, I grant you, but hardly indicative of a lack of character, I trust?

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: A handbag, Mr. Worthing? Found, you say? Really! One has quite enough trouble with illegitimate children as it is, without importing them via railway luggage! This is becoming increasingly distressing, and I must confess, highly irregular.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: I am engaged to Mr. Worthing, mamma.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Pardon me, you are not engaged to any one. When you do become engaged to some one, I, or your father, should his health permit him, will inform you of the fact. An engagement should come on a young girl as a surprise, pleasant or unpleasant, as the case may be. It is hardly a matter that she could be allowed to arrange for herself . . . And now I have a few questions to put to you, Mr. Worthing. While I am making these inquiries, you, Gwendolen, will wait for me below in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Mamma!

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: In the carriage, Gwendolen!

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Gwendolen, the carriage!

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Yes, mamma.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: You can take a seat, Mr. Worthing.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Thank you, Lady Bracknell, I prefer standing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I feel bound to tell you that you are not down on my list of eligible young men, although I have the same list as the dear Duchess of Bolton has. We work together, in fact. However, I am quite ready to enter your name, should your answers be what a really affectionate mother requires. Do you smoke?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Well, yes, I must admit I smoke.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I am glad to hear it. A man should always have an occupation of some kind. There are far too many idle men in London as it is. How old are you?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Twenty-nine.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: A very good age to be married at. I have always been of opinion that a man who desires to get married should know either everything or nothing. Which do you know?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: I know nothing, Lady Bracknell.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I am pleased to hear it. I do not approve of anything that tampers with natural ignorance. Ignorance is like a delicate exotic fruit; touch it and the bloom is gone. The whole theory of modern education is radically unsound. Fortunately in England, at any rate, education produces no effect whatsoever. If it did, it would prove a serious danger to the upper classes, and probably lead to acts of violence in Grosvenor Square. What is your income?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Between seven and eight thousand a year.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: In land, or in investments?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: In investments, chiefly.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: What between the duties expected of one during one’s lifetime, and the duties exacted from one after one’s death, land has ceased to be either a profit or a pleasure. It gives one position, and prevents one from keeping it up. That’s all that can be said about land.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: I have a country house with some land, of course, attached to it, about fifteen hundred acres, I believe; but I don’t depend on that for my real income. In fact, as far as I can make out, the poachers are the only people who make anything out of it.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: A country house! How many bedrooms? Well, that point can be cleared up afterwards. You have a town house, I hope? A girl with a simple, unspoiled nature, like Gwendolen, could hardly be expected to reside in the country.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Well, I own a house in Belgrave Square, but it is let by the year to Lady Bloxham. Of course, I can get it back whenever I like, at six months’ notice.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bloxham? I don’t know her.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Oh, she goes about very little. She is a lady considerably advanced in years.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Ah, nowadays that is no guarantee of respectability of character. What number in Belgrave Square?
